title: The Urban Heat Island Effect
topic: Why cities are warmer than surrounding countryside, and how planners are responding
passage:
Anyone who has driven from a city centre into open countryside on a summer evening may have noticed the temperature seem to drop as the buildings thin out. This is not imagination. Cities are measurably warmer than the rural land surrounding them, often by several degrees at night, a phenomenon meteorologists call the urban heat island effect. It was first documented systematically in the early nineteenth century by the amateur scientist Luke Howard, who compared temperature readings taken in London with those from nearby villages and found the city consistently warmer, particularly after dark.

The causes of the effect are now well understood, and they largely come down to how urban and rural surfaces handle solar energy differently. Vegetation and bare soil in the countryside absorb sunlight during the day but release much of that energy back through evaporation, a cooling process in which water turns to vapour and carries heat away with it. Cities have comparatively little vegetation and correspondingly little evaporative cooling. Instead, materials such as asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation efficiently during the day and, because they have a high thermal mass, release that stored heat slowly overnight, keeping urban air warmer long after the sun has set. Building geometry compounds the problem: tall structures packed closely together trap radiation between their walls in a phenomenon sometimes called the urban canyon effect, reducing how much heat can escape skyward compared with an open rural landscape.

Waste heat adds a further, if smaller, contribution. Air conditioning units, vehicle engines and industrial processes all release heat directly into the urban atmosphere as a by-product of their operation, and in dense city centres this waste heat can measurably raise ambient temperature, particularly in the narrow streets where it has limited opportunity to disperse. Reduced wind flow through densely built areas compounds the issue further still, since wind is one of the most effective natural mechanisms for redistributing and dissipating accumulated heat.

The consequences of persistently elevated urban temperatures extend well beyond simple discomfort. Heat-related illness and mortality rise sharply during heatwaves, and the effect is disproportionately felt in cities, where nighttime cooling — the period during which a heat-stressed body would normally begin to recover — is substantially reduced compared with surrounding rural areas. Epidemiological studies conducted after major European heatwaves have found that urban districts with the least vegetation and the highest density of heat-retaining surfaces recorded significantly higher mortality than greener districts experiencing an identical daytime temperature, isolating nighttime cooling, or its absence, as a decisive variable. Energy consumption also rises as buildings demand more air conditioning to compensate, which in turn adds further waste heat to the urban atmosphere, creating a feedback loop that intensifies the very problem it is responding to.

Addressing the heat island effect has become a genuine priority for urban planners, and the interventions being tested fall into a handful of broad categories. Reflective or 'cool' roofing materials, engineered to reflect a much higher proportion of incoming sunlight than conventional dark roofing, reduce how much solar energy a building absorbs in the first place, lowering both indoor cooling costs and the heat radiated back into the surrounding air. Urban tree planting restores some of the evaporative cooling capacity that dense development removes, while also providing direct shade that lowers surface temperatures on the pavement and buildings beneath a tree's canopy. Green roofs, in which a layer of soil and vegetation replaces conventional roofing material, combine both mechanisms, insulating the building beneath while releasing cooling moisture through the plants growing on top.

Singapore has become a widely cited example of heat island mitigation pursued at a city-wide scale, incorporating vertical gardens on building facades, extensive tree-lined boulevards, and building regulations that mandate a minimum proportion of greenery on new developments, sometimes calculated to exceed the footprint of the building itself once vertical and rooftop greenery are included. Researchers monitoring the programme have recorded measurable temperature reductions in the districts where these interventions have been most extensively applied, though they caution that isolating the contribution of any single measure from the combined effect of several implemented simultaneously remains difficult.

What makes the urban heat island effect particularly significant to planners is its interaction with global climate change. Rising background temperatures and the heat island effect operate through largely independent physical mechanisms, yet their consequences compound in the cities where both operate simultaneously. A heatwave that might have been merely uncomfortable a century ago can now push urban temperatures into a range associated with substantially elevated health risk, precisely in the built-up areas least equipped, structurally, to shed the resulting heat. For planners, the heat island effect is therefore no longer treated as an isolated curiosity of urban climate but as a hazard requiring deliberate, sustained architectural and infrastructural response.

questions.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage? Write TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if it contradicts it, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

questions.statement: Luke Howard compared London and village temperatures over a period of more than ten years.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says Howard "compared temperature readings taken in London with those from nearby villages", but it never says how long he did this for. The passage gives no length of time, so NOT GIVEN. Do not supply a number the text does not give.

questions.statement: Rural surfaces cool themselves partly through the evaporation of water.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that vegetation and soil release absorbed energy through evaporation, which it calls a cooling process. The statement paraphrases this as 'cool themselves partly through evaporation', so TRUE.

questions.statement: Waste heat from air conditioning and vehicles is the single largest cause of the urban heat island effect.
questions.explanation: The passage calls waste heat "a further, if smaller, contribution", which puts it below the causes described in the paragraph before it. The statement makes waste heat the largest cause, so the passage contradicts it: FALSE.

questions.statement: Studies after European heatwaves found mortality varied with vegetation levels even when daytime temperatures were the same.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes studies finding higher mortality in low-vegetation districts even at the same daytime temperature as greener ones, which matches the statement's claim exactly, so TRUE.

questions.statement: Singapore's building regulations always limit greenery to less than the footprint of the building.
questions.explanation: The passage says required greenery is "sometimes calculated to exceed the footprint of the building itself", contradicting the statement, so FALSE.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.question: What is the 'urban canyon effect' as described in the passage?
options: Heat escaping more easily upward in cities than in the countryside.
Tall, closely packed buildings trapping radiation between their walls.
Wind being channelled at high speed between skyscrapers.
Rivers running through the centre of major cities.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines the term right after naming it: buildings trapping radiation between their walls. This matches option B; wind speed and rivers are never linked to the term.

questions.question: According to the passage, why is nighttime cooling particularly important for health?
options: It is when most outdoor work and exercise takes place.
It is the period during which a heat-stressed body would normally recover.
It coincides with peak energy consumption in cities.
It allows air conditioning units to be switched off.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says nighttime cooling is when a heat-stressed body would normally recover, matching option B directly. The other options describe things the passage never links to nighttime cooling.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the feedback loop involving air conditioning?
options: Increased air conditioning use adds waste heat, which increases the need for further cooling.
Air conditioning has no measurable effect on outdoor temperatures.
Air conditioning use decreases as cities install more green roofs.
The feedback loop only occurs in cities without tree cover.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes exactly this cycle: more air conditioning adds waste heat, which raises the need for still more cooling. That is option A; the other options describe effects the passage never claims.

questions.question: What caution do researchers studying Singapore's programme raise?
options: That the temperature reductions recorded may not be genuine.
That isolating the effect of any single measure is difficult when several are applied together.
That vertical gardens have proven less effective than tree-lined boulevards.
That the programme has raised costs without any measurable benefit.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6 states this caution directly: it is hard to isolate one measure's effect when several are used together, matching option B. The other options describe doubts the passage does not raise.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

questions.sentence: Asphalt and concrete have a high ___, which allows them to release stored heat slowly overnight.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 uses the term 'thermal mass' right after 'high', which is where the gap in the question sentence sits.

questions.sentence: 'Cool' roofing materials are engineered to ___ a much higher proportion of incoming sunlight.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 uses the verb 'reflect' straight after 'engineered to', matching the gap's position in the question sentence.

questions.sentence: ___ replace conventional roofing material with a layer of soil and vegetation.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 opens the relevant sentence with 'Green roofs', which is the subject the question's gap is asking the learner to identify.

questions.sentence: Rising background temperatures and the heat island effect operate through largely independent physical ___.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph uses 'mechanisms' right after 'physical', describing how the two warming causes work through separate processes before their effects combine.
